audit_records.rationale: {"kind": "briefing", "translation_id": null, "briefing": {"psalm_id": "ps009", "translation_id": null, "background": {"authorship": "The heading calls this a מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד, a psalm associated with David. The preposition לְ can indicate authorship, dedication, or association; the heading supplies an attribution, not independent evidence establishing who composed the poem. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers commonly understand David as its author. Its other expressions concern a leader or musical director and the obscure עַלְמוּת לַבֵּן, variously understood as a musical instruction, a reference to a death, or something else. Radak discusses David’s victory over Goliath and reports Dunash’s proposal of an otherwise unknown enemy named Labben. These are interpretations of the heading, not events named in the body. Critical approaches can distinguish the original poet from the editors who supplied headings and arranged the collection; the commentary published under Ellicott regards authorship as unknown and proposes postexilic adaptation for congregational use. [Radak](https://www.sefaria.org/Radak_on_Psalms.9.1); [Ellicott commentary](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/9.htm).", "setting": "The poem itself names no king, battle, or date. It describes defeated enemies, destroyed cities, threatened sufferers, and YHWH’s presence in Zion. Its first-person speaker could be an individual or someone representing the community. A royal thanksgiving after victory is therefore plausible, but the speaker is never explicitly called king. A. F. Kirkpatrick proposes David’s victories, approximately the early tenth century BCE, comparing 2 Samuel 8. Radak’s Goliath interpretation and the proposal of Labben depend on readings of the heading. Rashi reports and rejects interpretations involving Absalom or Nabal; he instead reads the poem toward Israel’s future vindication and the downfall of Esau/Amalek. These are traditional identifications, not securely dated occasions. A later communal setting is also proposed: Ellicott’s commentary places adaptation after the exile, while Gunkel associates the mixed genres and alphabetic form with composition after about 500 BCE. Those literary arguments do not independently date a particular battle. Public worship is suggested by the performance heading and the summons to praise, but no specific festival can be established. [Kirkpatrick](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/9.htm); [Rashi](https://www.chabad.org/library/bible_cdo/aid/16230/jewish/Chapter-9.htm); [discussion of Gunkel’s dating arguments](https://dokumen.pub/download/a-word-fitly-spoken-poetic-artistry-in-the-first-four-acrostics-of-the-hebrew-psalter-studies-in-biblical-literature-1nbsped-9781433103889-1433103885.html).", "form": "This is thanksgiving interwoven with praise, statements of confidence, and petitions. Psalms 9–10 share an irregular Hebrew alphabetic pattern; the Septuagint and traditional Latin Psalter transmit them together as Psalm 9. Their original unity is widely accepted, though Kirkpatrick treats Psalm 10 as a companion composition. The pattern is not a regular one-letter-per-verse scheme: several opening lines begin with aleph, later units advance unevenly, and letters are missing or out of sequence. Translation can preserve its visible arrangement, explain it, or attempt an English analogue. Parallel lines repeatedly restate or develop a thought. There is no exact recurring refrain, but name, remembering/forgetting, knowing, returning, perishing, and forever bind the poem together. The two sets of gates in verses 14–15 form a pointed contrast. Higgaion and Selah occur together in verse 17; Selah closes verse 21. Their precise performance meanings are uncertain. All verse references here use Masoretic numbering. The supplied Hebrew has three omissions: verse 9 ends with an incomplete word whose full form is בְּמֵישָׁרִים; verse 13 omits the final written עניים/read עֲנָוִים; verse 19 omits written ענוים/read עֲנִיִּים after תִּקְוַת. These are gaps in the supplied extract, not evidence of gaps in the Masoretic text. [Complete Hebrew text](https://mechon-mamre.org/p/pt/pt2609.htm); [NRSVue’s structural note](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm+9&version=NRSVUE).", "themes": "After the heading, verses 2–3 promise wholehearted praise. Verses 4–7 connect the enemies’ defeat with the speaker’s vindication and the disappearance of their name and memory. Verses 8–11 contrast that disappearance with YHWH’s enduring rule and protection of the oppressed. Verses 12–13 invite public praise because God remembers victims of bloodshed. Verses 14–15 introduce, or recall, a plea for rescue so that the speaker can praise publicly. Verses 16–17 portray wrongdoing recoiling on its perpetrators. Verses 18–19 contrast the fate of those who forget God with God’s refusal finally to forget the needy. Verses 20–21 ask God to act and make nations recognize their human limitations. Thanksgiving and unresolved distress coexist; the choice of English verb forms can either preserve that tension or arrange it into a clearer sequence.", "reception": "Jewish interpretation includes historical deliverance, protection of the vulnerable, and future national vindication. Rashi’s future-oriented reading illustrates why past-looking Hebrew forms have sometimes been understood prophetically. Verse 13 is quoted in Av HaRachamim, the memorial prayer for murdered Jewish communities, giving its language about bloodshed a concrete history of communal lament. [Av HaRachamim text](https://www.yichabad.com/media/pdf/1126/sTJM11260532.pdf). Greek and Latin Christian readers usually encountered this poem together with Hebrew Psalm 10. The Greek heading concerning the son’s hidden things encouraged Augustine’s interpretation through Christ and hidden divine judgment; that interpretation should be distinguished from an established meaning of the Hebrew heading. [Augustine, Exposition on Psalm 9](https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801009.htm). Christian worship has also used the poem as thanksgiving and prayer for justice. Acts 17:31 closely echoes verse 9’s language about judging the world righteously, language also found in Psalms 96 and 98. It is not introduced as an explicit quotation uniquely identifying Psalm 9. That reception matters for recognizable wording, but does not itself settle this psalm’s tense or identify its speaker as Christ. witnesses.text: To the chief Musician upon Muthlabben, A Psalm of David. I will praise [thee], O LORD, with my whole heart; I will shew forth all thy marvellous works.
